items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: it was no small thing to have Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s... you had Sidney Bechet certainly

ctx.x: Well you must have been on your way to becoming pretty hip yourself, even maybe you didn’t even realize it.

I had no thoughts at that time of becoming in any way professionally involved in the music, but I was — it was like 52nd Street was in its final stages, but it was still alive and it was no small thing to have Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s and across the street maybe Charlie Parker if you were lucky and he was in town. And, you know, Billie Holiday at the Onyx Club. So there was still a lot going on. And this was, you know, still a vibrant time. There was downtown on weekends, there was the Stuyvesant Casino in…

not much more than a glorified messenger but I got to meet a lot of people and actually was talked into running for office at the American Newspaper Guild, a pretty left wing thing. I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president. That was that famous election when Truman — Truman and Dewey. And it was a great experience because I was working at Time Inc. I was at a nerve center there on election night, which was a studio where they were broadcasting, and there was a guy named H.V. Kaltenborn, who was —…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I saw Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s... Bechet was there as well. Bechet and Mezz played together... Bechet was not at all – Bechet could be very nasty to trumpet players, but he was very nice to Nat, whom he knew from Jimmy Ryan’s.

ctx.x: As a writer. There were people in California. First of all, his good friend whom he had traveled with was somebody who had – he had a porcelain factory in Austria which was taken over by his Christian partner, but they managed to tweak out money to him. Also my father had one good friend, a movie director named John Brahm, who is best known for a film noir called The Lodger, which is a Jack-the-Ripper film, which starred a good but unfortunate actor named Laird Cregar. I don't know if you knew him. Laird Cregar…

Then they had – of course it was important to arrange some kind of schooling for me. I enjoyed it, not having to go to school. I could see American movies for the first time in a long time. There was a boarding school outside of Stockholm where I then was sent along with a bunch of Danish kids my age and some Norwegians as well. Fairly recently – you know that we're on this jazz research list on the internet. There's one Norwegian there who is part of it, Arne Neegaard. We figured – he's the one who first figured…
